insights:what-we-underwrite:
Most of what reaches an investment committee is a good business in a market we do not understand, or a market we understand containing a business we cannot fix. Separating the two is most of the work.

Five tests. An opportunity has to pass all of them, and the fifth is where nearly everything stops.

One. Can we name the operator?

Not the sector, not the thesis — the person who will run it on a Tuesday in the second year, when the launch is over and the numbers are ordinary. If that name is a placeholder, we are underwriting a search, not a business, and a search is a different risk with a different price.

Two. Does the cash convert?

Revenue is a claim; collection is a fact. In several of our markets the gap between the two is measured in quarters, and a model that ignores it is not optimistic, it is wrong. We ask to see the receivables ledger before we ask to see the forecast.

Three. What does the second year cost?

First-year economics are almost always flattered — by launch pricing, by founder effort nobody is charging for, by a landlord's incentive. We underwrite year two, and we ask the seller to as well.

Four. Is the regulation stable, or merely quiet?

Healthcare and real estate are both licensed activities in every market we operate in. A licence that has not been tested is not the same as a licence that has been defended, and the difference only becomes visible under stress.

Five. What breaks if we are wrong?

The question is not whether the downside is survivable for SIRA. It is whether it is survivable for the operator, the staff and the partner who came in beside us.

This is the test most opportunities fail. A structure where our loss is capped and everyone else's is not may be defensible on paper and is still, in our experience, a bad way to build a second deal with the same people.

What this rules out

  • Businesses whose returns depend on a regulatory change that has not happened yet.
  • Assets we would have to sell into the same conditions that caused the problem.
  • Partnerships where our capital is the only thing at risk.

It rules out a great deal. That is the point of writing it down.
articles:inside-nairobi-s-diagnostic-ima:
Demand for advanced radiology is reshaping how healthcare investors think about East Africa, and the shift has been faster than most capital allocators expected.

Why now

Three things changed at once. Equipment financing became available locally rather than through offshore lessors, referring clinicians grew comfortable with cross-facility reporting, and patients began travelling shorter distances for a scan than for a consultation.

  • Imaging volumes rose faster than bed capacity.
  • Reporting turnaround, not machine count, became the binding constraint.
  • Insurers started reimbursing outpatient diagnostics directly.
The bottleneck was never the scanner. It was everything that had to happen before and after it.

What that means for operators

An operator entering the market now inherits the demand, but also inherits an expectation of turnaround that did not exist five years ago. Referrers have learned what a two-day report feels like and will not go back to a two-week one.

  1. Staff the reporting desk before the second machine.
  2. Contract with insurers early, and in writing.
  3. Publish turnaround times, then hold to them.

The part that is harder than it looks

Radiology is a people business wearing capital equipment. The scarce resource is a reporting radiologist willing to live within a reasonable distance of the facility, and no amount of imaging hardware substitutes for one. Every operator we have looked at underestimated this, and so did we, once.

Written by the SIRA Healthcare investment team.
insights:why-istanbul-remains-a-resilien:
Istanbul has survived more forecasts of its decline than almost any market we follow. It is worth being precise about which of its fundamentals are actually holding, and which two have quietly weakened.

What is holding

Household formation continues to run ahead of completions in the districts that matter, and the city keeps absorbing internal migration at a rate that no amount of new supply has yet met. Land in the well-connected corridors remains genuinely scarce, and scarcity of land is the only durable moat in residential development.

Construction cost has stopped being the story

For three years the input-cost line dominated every conversation. It no longer does. Costs remain high, but they are predictable, and a developer can price predictability.

What has weakened

  1. Exit liquidity at the top end. The buyer pool for large units has thinned, and it thinned faster than headline pricing suggests, because transactions that do not clear never appear in the index.
  2. The currency argument. International buyers who underwrote on a currency view rather than on rental yield have had a difficult two years, and that cohort is not returning at the same size.
A market can be resilient and still be a bad place to be under-capitalised. Those are separate statements.

Our own position is that Istanbul residential remains investable on rental fundamentals and delivery capability, and is not investable on a currency thesis. That has been our position for some time and the last eighteen months have not changed it.
articles:bridging-continents-through-sma:
A holding company is easy to describe and hard to justify. The description is that several businesses share an owner. The justification has to be that they are worth more together than apart, and most holding companies never actually make that argument.

The argument we make

SIRA operates across two geographies that are usually discussed separately — Türkiye and East Africa — and in sectors that are usually held by different kinds of investor. The connection is not thematic. It is operational.

  • Capital raised against a stabilised asset in one market funds development in the other.
  • A delivery team that has built in one regulatory environment learns faster in the second than a team starting cold.
  • Partner relationships travel. The introduction that opens a healthcare conversation in Nairobi frequently began somewhere else entirely.

What a group owes its companies

Three things, and they are unglamorous: patient capital, a functioning finance function, and the willingness to say no on their behalf when the group's balance sheet is what a counterparty is really after.

The test of a group is not what it adds in a good year. It is what it absorbs in a bad one.

What it does not owe them

Uniformity. Our healthcare business and our hospitality business have almost nothing in common operationally, and attempts to make them report identically would cost more in judgement than they would save in overhead.

Infrastructure for the next generation of growth is a phrase that means very little until someone specifies who maintains it. In our case the answer is the group, and that is the whole of the value proposition.
insights:the-cost-of-waiting:
Patient capital is a virtue right up to the point where it becomes an excuse. Three markets we looked at and did not enter have since moved decisively against a buyer, and it is worth being honest about what that cost.

The pattern

In each case the reasoning at the time was defensible: the regulatory position was unclear, the operator was unproven, the price implied a growth rate nobody could underwrite. In each case we were right about the specific risk and wrong about the direction of the entry price.

  1. Entry multiples rose while we waited for clarity that arrived eighteen months later.
  2. The best operators were taken by someone with a higher tolerance for ambiguity.
  3. The assets that remained available at our price were available for a reason.
Waiting is a position. It has a carry, and the carry is paid in opportunities you no longer get shown.

What we changed

We now distinguish between two kinds of unknown. An unknown that time will resolve is worth waiting on. An unknown that only operating will resolve is not — waiting produces no new information, it just makes the same decision more expensive.

That distinction has moved two of our last four investments earlier in their cycle than our previous framework would have allowed.
insights:hospitality-is-an-operating-bus:
Hospitality is sold to investors as real estate with a yield attached. It is not. It is a service business that happens to occupy a building, and the building is the least interesting part of the risk.

Why we staff before we buy

A hotel or a resort is a promise about a guest's experience on a specific night. That promise is kept by people who were hired, trained and retained months before the first booking. An operator brought in after completion inherits a building and a deadline and very little else.

You cannot retrofit a service culture into a property that has already opened badly. The reviews arrive faster than the training does.

What it has cost us

Twice. Both times the sequence was the same: an attractive asset, a construction programme that ran to schedule, and an operating team assembled too late to shape the thing they were being asked to run. Both recovered, and both took a full season longer than they should have.

What we do now

  • The general manager is appointed before the fit-out specification is signed.
  • Service standards are written by the person who will be held to them.
  • The opening date moves for readiness. It has moved.

None of this is novel. It is simply expensive to learn any other way.
articles:notes-from-a-year-of-building-i:
Running an Istanbul development team and a Nairobi clinical team out of one investment committee sounds like a governance problem. In practice the governance was the easy part.

What actually took the time

Not the strategy, and not the reporting. What took the time was the ordinary friction of two organisations that were awake at different hours, held different assumptions about what a decision is, and had never met.

  • A development team treats a date as a commitment. A clinical team treats it as a forecast subject to a regulator. Both are correct in context.
  • An approval that takes an afternoon in one market takes a committee cycle in the other, and neither team believed the other until they watched it.
  • Written English is a second language for most people involved, and a great deal of apparent disagreement was vocabulary.
The two teams did not need to work the same way. They needed to stop being surprised by each other.

Three things we would do differently

  1. Put them in a room in the first month, not the sixth. The cost of the flights was recovered several times over in decisions that stopped needing three rounds.
  2. Write down what a decision is. Who makes it, what makes it final, and what re-opens it. We assumed this was shared and it was not.
  3. Stop translating culture into process. Our first instinct was a new reporting template. It solved nothing and consumed a quarter.

What worked

One overlapping hour, held every week, with an agenda neither team owned. It is a small thing and it did more than the template.
articles:land-assembly-and-the-patience-:
One Istanbul block. Six years. Four deals that nearly ended the whole thing, and one that actually did before it was revived.

The shape of the problem

Assembly is not buying land. It is buying the last parcel, and everything before that is positioning for a negotiation you cannot begin until you are visibly committed. The moment your intention becomes obvious, your remaining counterparties reprice.

Every assembly has a parcel whose owner understands exactly what they are holding. The question is only whether you find out early or late.

Four near-endings

  1. An inheritance dispute that froze a central parcel for fourteen months and could not be accelerated by any amount of money.
  2. A neighbouring owner who agreed terms twice and withdrew twice, on both occasions after our own financing had been committed against the timetable.
  3. A zoning consultation that would have reduced the developable area by a fifth, resolved only because the consultation itself lapsed.
  4. A partner who wanted out at the point of maximum illiquidity, which is the only point at which anyone ever wants out.

What we learned about financing patience

Assembly capital and development capital are different instruments and should not come from the same facility. We funded the first three years on terms that assumed a development timetable, and spent the fourth renegotiating them. The lesson was expensive and is now structural: assembly is equity, development is debt, and mixing them puts a clock on a process that does not respond to clocks.

Part of an occasional series on how SIRA Real Estate actually operates.
insights:what-good-partnership-looks-lik:
Partnerships are underwritten on the pitch and judged on the second year. By then the launch energy is gone, the original champions have often moved on, and what remains is whatever was actually written down.

What we measure

  • Response time on bad news. Not on good news — everyone is fast with good news. The interval between a partner discovering a problem and telling us is the single most predictive number we track.
  • Whether the people who signed are still involved. Continuity is not sentimentality; it is the difference between a relationship and a contract.
  • How the first disagreement was handled. Every partnership has one in the first eighteen months. How it went tells us more than the previous eighteen months of reporting.
A partner who brings you a problem in week one is worth more than a partner who brings you a solution in month six.

What we stopped measuring

Meeting frequency. We used to treat a regular cadence as a health indicator and it is not — some of our best relationships are quiet for a quarter and then entirely open for a week, and some of the worst were impeccably scheduled.

The uncomfortable one

We also ask whether the partnership has cost the partner anything yet. If it has not, we do not yet know what it is worth. That question has ended two conversations early, which we consider a good outcome for everyone.
insights:istanbul-residential-a-ten-year:
A ten-year view of Istanbul residential is really three views — demographics, currency, and construction cost — and they do not move together.

Demographics

The most reliable of the three. Household formation in the city continues to outpace completions in the connected districts, and internal migration has been remarkably insensitive to every shock of the last decade. If nothing else in this note holds, this will.

Currency

The least reliable, and the one most often used to sell the market to international buyers. A currency thesis is a bet on the timing of a repricing, not on the asset, and it has produced most of the disappointment we have seen from foreign investors in this market.

If your return requires the currency to do something specific, you have bought a macro position with a building attached.

Construction cost

The one that will decide yields between now and 2034. Costs have stabilised at a level that materially changes what can be built profitably in the mid-market, and we expect that to push supply toward either the top of the market or genuinely dense product, with relatively little in between.

Where that leaves yields

  1. Rental yields in connected districts hold or improve, on supply constraint rather than on rent growth.
  2. Capital values become more dispersed by district than they have been.
  3. The mid-market gap widens, and it is the most interesting place to be building.

None of this is a forecast we would underwrite a single asset against. It is the frame we use to decide which questions to ask about one.
